His answer is, " because it is the best, for the reason that the eow, in Denmark calve between the months of Novendar and January, and they and their produce are much better cared for than inane other producing country in Europe. The butter is made on estates or large farms ' where are usually kept from 100 to 2so cows, and in some cases even more A person is also kept who has had some years' training in the preparation of milk for butter-making ' purposes. Further, the lucre:ism' demand for Danish butter has brought prices gradmilly to such a height that the farmers find it pays theta to teed the cattle with their corn, in addition to the most celebrated feeding stuffs that can be obtained in Eng,land or America. The hest Danish hotter will yet grow finer by degrees, and the second quality, now selling in London at about 1300. to 140 w per cwt., will greatly improve. The latter is made in the fume style as Normandy butter, viz., front email farm, where from four to : twenty cows are kept. The stock of cattle in Demnark is about 02 1,000 milch cows over two years; 865,C00 young cattle under two years, 135,000 oxen, meetly fat cattle, for export. Denmark exports about 10,000 easks of butter per week, averaging 80Ib. net, out of which at present about 4,0a0 are ,not to London. It is interesting to note that the Pled Wagtail is one of our peculiarly English birds, being one of the few Euro- pean PINNA, which is common in the British Islands and rare in other parts of the Continent ; this, at least, is true as regards the breeding season. In the Smith of England faire resklent bird, though the numbers decrease hi very severe weather, when the bird probably migrates, for iv Weatern Scotland it may be lokaal uon as it regular migra- tory specie., o it has been stated to disappmr entirely from its summer haunts in the outer Hebrides, where it returns again in spring. It was at one time supposed to be only a native of Great Britain, and is even to this day heat known by the name of -11,4nrilleg yertrdli, having been thus called IT Mr. Gould, after the celehnded English naturalist Ter- rell. In the part of Berkshire near Cooldmm, where many of the writer's personal experiencm of birds have been gathored, the Wagtail is the especial victim of the Cuckoo, many of who eggs he has found in the nest of the Pied " Dishwasher," as he is familiarly called in 111.11 and in most parts of the country. Go one occastam the nest was louilt in the mould of a flower-basket tin the lawn at Pomo., near Cooklon, and at some distance from the edge of tha wood- work. There the nmt was found by Mr. Briggs, the head ordener on the estate, one of the best field-oat uralists known to the writer, as indeed is tostilied lay the frequent refer- ences to his olwervations in Mr. Clohld's "Birds of tmeat Britain," and to this day his untimely death is deplored by all who knew hint. The Cuckoo's eot WM duly point ml out be Mr. Briggs, but eo exactly alike in colour was it to the , oiher eggs of the foster-parent, that the writer expressed the strongest doubts unto its being really anything but it rather large Wagtail's egg. Time, however, proved the contrary,' and it V,ar trot long before the nest, which was rather a rudely constructed affair, placed in a hollow depression in the mould of the flower-basket, was completely tilled by a hungry,yellow,gapingyoungCuckoo,who, on being hatched, disposed in the usual corollate way of his foster-brothers and sisters. These were food, curiously enough, lying dead on the grass at some little distance from the flower-basket, and the oumtion which was asked was. whether the old Cuckoo real,/ is the unregenerate deserter of its offspring that it is generally made out to be, or whether it still takes a parental intelot in the young birds, which it nevertheless leaves to the rare of foster-parents to bring up. Mr. Briggs always held the idea that thy Cuckoo MU 1101 devoid of this natural instinct, and he imagined that the removal of the young Wan,rtails was the work of one of the parents of the young Cuckoo. It is, however, probable that the old Wagtails, finding the dead bodies of the nestlings left on the mould, themselves acted on undertakers, and carried them to some little distance. All the time that the nest was under exami- nation the Wagtails. were in close attendance, with their mouths full of mtertallars and insects, evincing the utmost distreas, and running about on the edge of the flower-basket. Mr. Gould oven says that they will fly in the face of any one atteutpting to remove their unwieldy foster-child, and that when the latter is rmtored to the nest they " will evince their joy by fondling arid dancing mound it, Imping over its back, amt exhibiting many other demonstrations of delight."—" Cassell's Nee Ilistory."

Attracted and much interested, like ever; other travel- ler, I went to see the Sultan go "it, state " to pray. The day was Friday, the time noon, the mosque selected for the oceasion that near the garden entrance to at summer pal-tee. The intervening roadway was lined With troop whilst the space immediately in front of the mosque was, in addition, occupied by. strong guard of honour, a military band, a body of trumpeters, and a number of officers, amongst whom were several very tall fussy negvoes, who appeared to be great favourites with all. They were eunuchs, T was toll Behind the ground held by the troops was a dew, eitient, .4ml-humoured crowd of cith.ens. It was not until an hone after the announced time that his Majesty screwed up his courage sufficiently to show him- self fore few minutes to his people. Then, at length, the garden gates were opened; the troops stood to attention, and a hush of expectation fell on all that vast multitude. As the meteor approached, we sow the Sultan on horselwek in the midst of a compact body-guard of high State officials, all of whom were on foot. The distance front gate to mosque was about Ino yards. In lot's than two minutes from its appearance the procession came too hat before the mosque. The troops presented arms, the trumpets , soundfsl, the hand played, and most of us unbelievers un- covered. The Sultan dismounted hurriedly, as if afraid to be looked at, and dragged his faltering legs up the carpeted steps of the musque. He raised his hands to his fare, o,f if timing or saluting them. There was a rapturous shout, and he woe gone. From first to last he had not been visible for more than two or three minutes, aml ill the last few seconds of those two minutes the present state of the Tur- f kish empire MIA reflected before our eyes as from a mirror. That central, timid. corpse-like man, with the bloodless face and the nerveless gait, that is the Sultan—the tuber of Turkey. Those splentlidlydresassl officers, whose breasts sparkle with decorations, whose bodies are no burly, and whose face, look so nellnll2l 311 d possion-swayed, they are the great State officers, who rule the ruler of Turkey. They ; all hate and fear each other they all love the some thing. Their country ? NO ; but power and money. These are their gods. For these they are starving the army and plun- dering their fellow-subjects—in short, destroying their country. And their Sultan, he who is so amiable, hos, like the Emperor of Russia, such goal intentions," What of him? Miserable. cadaverous being, Ile is the slave ell what- ever clique of Paellas is in ismer. And those troops, what a grand physierfe they Imre! That cannot he hid. though there uniforms are worn, torn, and threadbare. With what fervent devotion they shout as their poppet Sultan turns his pale face and twitching hands towards them for a mo- ment before he takes refuge in the mosque ! And look be- yond the troops at the great array of thin, keen, attentive faces. They belong to the citizens of Constantinople. Their garments are rags, their stomachs are empty ; and yet, when I they see their Sultan and his magnificent suite, they shoot as devotedly as do the troops. In any other capitoel in the world both troops and citizens would fraternbfe and destroy that ntagnificent " ring " of plundering nICIIIIS—what re- strains them in the intensity of their superstitiotis venera- tion for the head of their religion, and that natural suhntis- sivenem to those in authority which is no admirable a characteristic of the Turk.—" To Constantinople by the Shipka Pus," in Plackenerl'A Mager.rine.

The limits of age are ID and 25, and the subjects for examination are writing, orthography, arithmetic to vulgar and docimal fractions), and English composition. A fee of 15s, is to be paid at the examination. The starting salary for oubdoor custom officers, with the exception of London an Liverpool, is £55 per year, with ! Is. on Sundays, when employed, until a maximum of £7O is reached. The salaries for Ist class officers in London begin at £3O, and ex4nd to £lOl., and those of 2nd class officers begin at £7l and extend to £Bl. In Liverpool the salaries are—firet. clam £B6 to £lOO, and, second class, £7l to £Ol. , The position of examining officer is open for them to coin- ! pete for after three years of approved service. THE ALLEGED MURDER OF A MOSEL'S DAUGHTER.

The trial of James Lewis Paine for the murder of Miss Maclean, on the 17th of November Net, was concluded before Mr. Justice ;Hawkins, at the Central Criminal Court, on ; Toeslay. The case for the defence and prosecution having I concluded on Monday, the learned Judge commenced his ; summing up. Ile said that, both in the inters,oo of the public at large as well as iu that of the deceased woman, a pLblic investigation of the circumstances by which she !net , her death was imperatively necessary. With the jury would rest the grave responsibility of fixing the blame upon or of exonerating the primmer, and he implored them 000 00 pay any attention to anything which be might say if it should not commend itself to their conscience and understamling. But he also warned them not to allow theocrats. tube influ- enced by sympathy for either party. It would be for them to decide whether, after having heard the law on the subject, the prisoner was guilty of m.slaughter, or whether they constlereti him innocent of both crimes. The law Le laid down by the learned Attorney-lieneral commended itself to his mind. If a person administered to another anything that would destroy Ids or which he knew would be deleterious to life, with the object of destroying it, and thereby did take ' life, he was guilty of murder. That neglect which was re- quired to convict a mon o,f manslaughter was not ordinary neglect, but gross, culpable negligence, undefined by law, but which must be detinsl by the jury. 11, 00 the other , hand, they found that this culpable neglect did not ; cadet, then it was their duty to had the num , innosent. In order to make an administer- ing" in the eye of the law, there most be some Codes step taken he did not mean necesmfrily by himself. : If he 4he judge) were to see a person take a tumbler of ; poison and drink it, he would not be amenable to the law, for he was not Loynd to protect a &ranger from his own dependent acts ; but if he was to say to him, "take this,- ; and he took it and dropped down dead, then he would come I within the pale of the law, inasmucha he ofiersi an induce- ment. His lordship theu reverted to the facts of the cam, and pointed out the relations which exisnd between the prisoner and the deceased. Referring to the statements mad- by Fanny Matthews, he said it would be for them to decide whether they were credible or not. Alluding to the evidence of Pr. Shepherd, that it woo always most difficult to restraiti a person who had once become addicted to drink, the learned judge remarked it might also be mid that it was the duty of persons in charge of such a person to prevent stimulants being placed in his or her way. The theory of the prosecution, he said, was that the object of prisoner was to posseau himself of the deceased's money and property, and that when he had an possessed himself of her money he no longer cared for her life. It was not because the proses cution made the suggestion they were to take it for granted. They must look and see whether such a theory was justified by the evidence.—The jnry retired at 4.38 p.m., and re- named into court at 5.511 with a verdict of manslaughter.— The primmer said he wee absolutely innocent of havit g done any injury to the little lady, whom he had known be 15 nears. lie would have called witnesses if he had nnt felt sure that his innocence would have been proved. He made a long statement explaining his connection with deceased The Judge addressed the prisoner at coneiderable length, Mating that if be had been found guilty of murder he would have expiated his crime. He would be sentenced to penal Servitude for the term of bra nature/ life.

div.head: OBSTRUCTION DEBATE.
div.p: THE OBSTRUCTION DEBATE.

, Sime the opening of Parliament public business on the whole has been making tolerably fair prugreas. We have bad an Irish Distress Bid and several measures of no important character, and on subjecta that require urg. nt attention have been in Parlia- mentary language " advanced a stage." But we fear that this aatinfactory state of things is now coming to an end, and that in all probability between this and Easter there will be very little of useful Irgialation to , record. On Thurelay evening Sir Stafford Northeime moved the resolution on the subject of Parliamentary obetruction of which be had given notice on the pre- vious Monday, and from all appearances there will be a long and wearieme struggle between the obstruc- tioniata and the Government before the debate is eon. chided. In the event of Sir Stafford Northeote succeeding in the end in passing hit rem/Intim, and in making it a standing order of the House instead of a mere erosional order, it may he mid that the time occupied will not be wasted, inasmuch HP it would clear the way for the next Parliament to engage in ! practical work without lot or hindrance. But how I far Sic Stafford Northcote'a proposal is calculated to I . obtain the general support of the House of Commos and of the recognises, leaden, of the Opposition haa yet to be sc-en. All must admit that the change pro- ! posed in a very serious one and one that looks so much like an interferonoo with freedom of discussion that it behoving the Oppositios to regard it with jealous attention. The most important feature of the resolution is the Mange that it would make in the relative positions of the speaker and the House of Commons. The speaker of the House of Commons is not invented with even the same kind of authority as the chairman of an ordinary meeting or as the preeident of a legislative assembly, his function being merely to rule on the points of order to which his attention is called, and to give effect to the wishre of the Honey. The House of C 4132113.8 has always been most jealous of placing anything like initiative authority in the hands of the Speaker. It is not. for instance, his business to call a member to order, but only to give his decision on points of order. But should Sir Stafford Nerthcoteht resolution be adopted in inn entirely it will henceforth , be the part of the Speaker to name any member guilty of an offence against order. This being done, and a motion being made. the Speaker will then have the power to put the question that the offending member be " suspended," from taking any part in the proceedings of the House during the remainder of that ample sitting. So that, should the resolution be retried, the Obstructionists may here. after be able to Loaet that they have had the honour, or dishonour, of bringing about an important change i3l the very comtitutim of the British House of Com- mons. However effiescions, therefore, the proposal of the Government might privy as a remedy for the immediate evil complained of it is impmsible to regard the passing of suck a measure with feelings of unmixed satisfaction. It is a matter moot difficult to deal with, inasmuch as there is the danger of the remedy that permanently introduced, doing more harm than the disease that it ioioterdedto cure. For while on the one side, as ull must admit, It is most important that ouch an , assembly as the House of CUMMOUS should be a very model of order and decorum, and that there should be ales capable of restraining members fine- "ex atiously opposing and hindering the transaction et business, it is also most important that every possible safeguard should remain in force to secure the utmoat freedom for fair discussion, and for fair and legitimate opposi- . tion on the part of a minority, or even the section of a minority hewer small and insignificant. A tyran- nical majority," suck m one sometime sees in muni- cipal assemblies, and that has its own way irrespective of the viewe of the minority of its members is a kind ' of thing towards which the British House of Com- mons has usually exhibited a decided antipathy and I it would boa dangerous and disastrous experiment to do away with the various " forms of the House " that! , enable minorities at timen to offer a very determined I opposition to measures to which they are oonseienti- ously oppoeed. The queetion before the Home is how to represa obstruction of a thoroughly mare. on. , able and vexatious character, and when it takes the raise oTtinifoorm nse.of Th"lkattit'go say'tatinmheonowithibnletmheember, well acquainted with the rules of the Boner, can keep strictly within those rules, and yet go on talking for hours, net for the purpme of convincing by his arra. : ments, but for the mere purpose of preventing the I transaction of the legitimate business that is under discussion. The supporters of the resolution now be- fore the House are apparently of opinion that there in lonly one way of putting a stop to the talker against , time, and that is by silencing him, in the way de- scribed, for the remainder of the day's sitting It will at once be seen that it is a proposal that will put extraordinay powers into the hands of the Speaker. He it is who will have to sit in judgment as it were, .a when an honourable member begins to wander from his subject, instead of having his ears greeted by the familiar en. of "question," he will be inter- rupted by the Speak, informing him that he is guilty of obstruction, and on a motion being

!made the offeuder would be put to silence: : for the remainder of the night. The demand for local consamp- tion is still small, for although works generally throughout the district are getting busier, consumers in most eases are so well covered for the present that it ir exceptional when they are compelled to come into the market for raw material. and the prices now asked do not io,tuco hem to anticipam requirements by entering into speculative forward purehases. For shipment there is al.o less pressing inquiry, but the falling off in this direction is still believed to be only tem. porary, and a considerable development of business is anticipated next month when the spring shiptnents coo,- In the finishe,h iron trade there is no material change to notice with regard to the position of makers. bell merchants and dealers are soared, as Arrn as they were, and I good ordinary bus deliverol into the Manchester district have been toffered at £8 10n. to £8 15s. per ton ; hoops retnain at £lO halo £lO 10s. per ton. A few of the large engineering firms are busy, but ' Flee majority of the works are still short of orders, although in most cams they are doing more than they were and the number of men out of employment in considerably less, the returns of the Amalgamated Society of Engineers showing that them are 400 men less on donation than at this time last year, and the number of men on the books is being gradually reduced week by week. RUNCORN, WESTON, AND HALTON WATERWORKS' COMPANY. The half-yearly meeting of the proprietors was held on Monday afternoon at the offices, Public Ball, Runcorn. Mr. John Brundrit, J.P., chairman of the Company, presided; and there were elm present Messrs. Thomas Bankes, John Sitnpson, John Rigby, E. Timmins, limes Shaw, Philip Speakonni, W. Rigby, T. Norman, W. Whittaker,lT. hooker, and W. F. Sal held (secretary). From the report and statement of accounts, which it was agreed to take as read, it appeal-id that the revenue account shows a balance of £1.518 4s. Sd., inclusive of the deprecia- tion fund, out of which the directors recommend a dividend to be paid of 24 per cent. per annum, free of income -.ax, which will absorb £258 10s., the depreciation hind £soo,and carry a balance forward of £757 I4s. &I. to the next half. year. . . . .

„ The CHAIRMAN moved the adoption of the report and statement of accounts, and mid lid bad every reason to ion. grabble the Company on the steady- progress which had been mole. They would see that the revenue account was steadily increasing, or whilst in the half-year ending June 301', 1879, the sum re,ived for water was £1,373 3s. 70., the amount received for the six months ending December 31st, 1879, was £2,000 lb. Sid. These figuree showed that in that very short tirne the revenue account of tha Cmnpany had very nearly doubled. That waa ono reason why they had been able to declare a dividend lathe shareholders, and they hoped that in future they would be able to inermse that payable this half-year. The revenue account showtd a balance of £1,510 as. M., and the directors recommend that a dividend should he Nid at the rate 0( 2* per cent. per annum. The speaker then re- ferred to the great expense which hail hi-on entailed upon the Company, owing to people keeping their taps running during the winter's frost, which conduct he condemnor' in unineasured terms. The interest which had to he paid on the guarantee stock was gradually decreasing, as they could now, in some inatances, get the meneY they ',Mired at 4f per cent, instead of 5,0 s at the formation of the Craw pany. Ile was glad to my that the expenses did not in. crease, although the revenue was m much in advance of what it had bem in the past. The expenses for the half- year ending June 39th, 1879, were £390 4e. (hi., but for December 3lat, 1379, they were on:y £532 18.. fid,thus showing that, though the Company were pumping more water, they were paying less for expenses. No doubt one reason for this was OA the low price of fuel and iron had allowed them to make contraets at prices which had been remunerative to them. The Company had made a very good contract for foci, which would continue in force until February next year, BO that the directors did not anticipate there would lw any considerable rise in the expenses for the ner! half-year. . . .

Mr. P. SPHAMMAN proposed that a vote of thanks should be passed to the Chairman and directors for the manner in which they had conducted the business of the Company during the year and also that an honorarium of MO Iv. placed at the dispoxil of the directors for their services during the last ten years. Mr. THOMAS NORMAN seconded the motion, and remarked that he thought the sum ought to he 1100 at least, consider- Mg that there won no fewer than six directors. The motion was passed. The CHAIRMAN, after consalting with the other directors present, said that, whilst duly anpreciating their kindness, they felt it would be better to leave SUCII a propos,' over for another half year, untd the dividend WAS further im- proved. The dividend this half year had !won placed at per cent., owing Co the directors beinto of opinion that it was well for the shareholders to have some fund to fall back upon in case of any accident or extra expenses being in- curred.

THE CORACLE.—AII this part of the Wye over which we have travelled is famed as a salmon river. A curious'. sur- vival" of ancient days which cannot fail to be noticed in the coracle, still used on the Wyr, a boat which probably has descended with little alteration from the times of our British forefathers. It is commonly called • "coracle,” but in these parts the word is al. alteresi into thoracie" and "truckle." Boata of this kind are used still in various districts, of Wales !and on the west co.mt of Ireland they even floated on the I Tigris in the days of flerodotus. Pliny alm tells ai, goof- ' lug All old historian, that the Britons took voyages sin days long- ton certain island otllnd Mictis—in wicker-work boats covertd with hides. Pretty much in thin way the coracle is still made. It is in slur. like a rather fiat half walnut- ! shell, the frame of sticks or laths, forming a sort of open !lattice-work, covered with canvas (or now sometimm sine) instead of hide, with a pLank across for a seat. It is pro- pelled by .1 paddle, and is so light as to be carried with ease lon the back. An inexperienced utvigator will probably find It at first better suited for putting him into than keeping him out of the seater, aa these cockle-shells-are very crank. I Our Urn Country for Febnary.

The annual meeting of the Brunswick Sunday School teachers took place on Monday evening. The annual report of I 9 Carruthers, mftlical of ficer of , health for the Halton and NVeston districts, showed that during the year there hod been 181 births anal 99 deaths in the district, making o birth rate of 37.6 per 1.000, and a! death rote of 206 per 1,000. The number of blithe in 1578 was 197, or 410 per 1,000, and the number of deaths 113. or 235 per 1,000. The decrease in the death rote WAS principally from dieeases of the lungs, the deaths from those diseases in 1878 being 30, whilst in 1879 there were only 15. The report also 'showed that a gradual improvement was being made hi the condition of the cottage property of the district, though much still remained to be done—The annual report of the medical racer of the Great Budsrorth district, Dr. Wdlett, showed that the deaths had been 77, and the births 132. 'file death rate in the Daresbury dis- trict had born 36-17 males and 19 females, being a mortality at the rate of 13 per 1,000. The total births had been 66, against 65 last year. The report concluded by calling attention to the scorcity of drinking water in the several townships of tired liudworth, especially Antrobto and I,ower Whitley. SHOCKING Arnagsgran SUICIDE AT Wasangaros.— On Wednesday last, a man named James Rogers, game- keeper, of Cutcheth, made a determined attempt at suicide at the Mill Stone Inn, Sankey-street. He went into a Mall room off Golborne.street, shortly after four o'clock, and the landlord, Mr. Farnw..rth having heard someone ..nter, went into the room and there saw Rogers leaning with hie head on a table, and blood pouring on the door front a fearfu gash in his throat, and in one hand was the razor with which he had inflicted the wound. The police were at Mee com- municated with and medical aid sent for. Drs. T. S. Smith, Spioks, and Booth (of Farnsworth. who happened to be in company th Mr. Spinks at the time), were soon on the spot. They found that the gash HU Of a serious character. node, nothing could be done with him there, hie removal to the Infirmary moo ordPred. Inspector Froffit had the man conveyed there on a stretcher, and a horrible sight was presented to the large crowd which assembled in the street, as the man threw off the coverings whilst he was being carried, and made an effort as if to get off the stretcher, toe causing a freeh effusion nf blood and exposing his wound. Front the fearful quantity of blood lost in the smoking-room, where he made the attempt on his life, there seemed on poseibility that he could recover but as soon as he got to the Infirmary he received every atten- tion attic hands of Dr. Richmond, and on making inquiries last evening there seems every probability of his recovery, if he can he prevented from injuring himself further. For , icerpOee 3 police-conetable has been engaged watching him constantly. The act wes evidently premeditated, from the fact that in his pocket was found a letter addressed to hie sister, Mrs. Brian, Brook House Farm, Culcheth. which was as follows ,—" Dear sister Good bye. God bless you. Take care nf the cowsand calves. Farewell to you all. MY head is bad. IM the hem you can." It is said aka he his been in a despondent state of mind for P.M creek% owing to domestic difficulties.
